slides.title: clim°: storm insurance for Uniswap v4 LPs
slides.text: DeVinci Blockchain × TOKEN2049 Origins Hackathon, 6 to 8 October 2026. clim°. Storm insurance for Uniswap v4 LPs. Built on Chainlink and Uniswap.
slides.notes: Hi, I am Sofiane, from DeVinci Blockchain. This is clim°: storm insurance for the people who provide liquidity on Uniswap v4, the liquidity providers, or LPs. I built it on Chainlink CRE and Uniswap v4 for TOKEN2049 Origins. Keep the pink spiral in mind: it is the same storm that runs on the app's screen, because the whole idea is that the fee follows the weather.

slides.title: Where the idea comes from
slides.text: Fables on Robinhood Chain. Liquidity providers earned fees. Arbitrage took back 75 to 105 %. Bar chart: fees earned; lost to arbitrage, 75 to 105 % of them. ETH/USDG, 14 days. Pre-hackathon research, 30 Sept 2026.
slides.notes:
This idea did not start on a whiteboard. Before the hackathon, I measured 14 days of Fables' ETH/USDG pool on Robinhood Chain against three external prices that agreed. Depending on the method, arbitrage took back 75 to 105 % of the fees the liquidity providers earned. Researchers call that loss loss-versus-rebalancing, or LVR. This is pre-hackathon research, not a result of the hack. It is why clim exists: the fee did not keep up with the weather. Every AMM has this problem; Fables' pool is simply where I measured it.

Sources (not read aloud): research note dated 2026-09-30, summarized in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-06-clim-design.md section 1.3 (external mids from Coinbase, Lighter and Hyperliquid).

slides.title: The problem: the same fee in calm and in storm
slides.text: Same fee in calm and in storm. Two columns, calm and storm: fees earned are the same; lost to arbitrage is small in calm and larger than the fees in a storm. Illustrative, same trading volume: double the volatility, about four times the loss.
slides.notes:
When ETH jumps on Binance, arbitrage bots buy from the pool at the old price, and the LP pays the gap. That loss grows with the square of volatility, so a storm costs the LP several times what a calm day does. Yet the pool charges the same fee in both. These bars are illustrative, not measured: same trading volume, volatility doubled, about four times the loss.

Sources (not read aloud): Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden and Zhang (2022), Automated Market Making and Loss-Versus-Rebalancing, arXiv:2208.06046 (LVR grows with the square of volatility).

slides.title: The idea: the fee follows the weather
slides.text: The fee follows the weather. LPs sell insurance. clim makes the premium rise in a storm. Chart: fee per swap against ETH volatility per year: calm, 5 bp; 100 %, 10.95 bp; storm, 225 %, 24.63 bp. 1 bp = 0.01 % of each trade.
slides.notes:
An LP is an insurer: it sells protection to traders, and the fee is its premium. That is the storm insurance on the cover: with clim, the premium finally covers the storm. When the market is calm, the fee is the pair's usual tier, 5 basis points, that is 0.05 % of each trade, so traders pay what the pool next door charges. Above about 46 % annualized volatility, the fee rises in proportion: 10.95 basis points at 100 %, 24.63 at 225 %. This is the exact schedule of the hook deployed on Sepolia.

Sources (not read aloud): README section "Fee schedule", computed from shared/params.json (P* = 30 %, floor 500 pips, k = 1).

slides.title: How it works: nobody changes the fee by hand
slides.text: Nobody changes the fee by hand. 4 exchanges, then Chainlink CRE (measures the weather every 30 s), then the risk desk (one number, on-chain), then the Uniswap v4 hook (prices every swap). Sepolia testnet. CRE in simulation.
slides.notes:
Every 30 seconds, a Chainlink CRE workflow reads one-minute ETH prices from Coinbase, Kraken, Binance and Hyperliquid. At least three of them must agree, and it turns them into one number: how stormy the market is right now, the 15-minute realized volatility. That number is written on-chain to my risk desk contract. On every swap, Uniswap v4 calls my hook, which reads the desk and returns the fee for that swap only: no keeper, no admin call, no fee-update transaction. On a Chainlink network of nodes (a DON), the nodes would agree on the median and sign one report; today one simulated node does it, on the Sepolia testnet.

Sources (not read aloud): workflow cre/risk-desk/workflow.ts (cron 30 s, HTTP, ConsensusAggregationByFields median, EVMClient.writeReport); contracts/src/RiskDesk.sol and contracts/src/ClimHook.sol (beforeSwap with OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG); DON deploy access requested on 2026-10-06 and not granted during the hackathon, so the DON deployment was cut.

slides.title: The storm of 4 February 2026
slides.text: The storm of 4 February 2026. Chart from 12:00 to 16:00 UTC: ETH volatility per year (pink, between 34 % and 296 %); the clim fee (blue, from 5 to 32.4 bp); a fixed-fee pool with the same average fee (dashed, 15 bp). Real Binance prices at the deployed parameters (lab replay).
slides.notes:
This is a real storm: 4 February 2026, replayed with Binance prices at the parameters of the deployed hook. Volatility, in pink, moved between 34 % and 296 % a year. clim's fee, in blue, followed it from 5 to 32 basis points. A fixed-fee pool charging the same average fee, 15 basis points, stayed flat. I also replayed this window on Sepolia, through a second CRE loop and a second desk flagged REPLAY.

Sources (not read aloud): lab/out/replay-2026-02-04.json; replay desk 0x4b843dc3A7ec6202d2337cdeF8C67a0F10f24746 on Sepolia (459 reports, 2026-10-06 16:57 to about 21:00 UTC).

slides.title: Does it work: LPs lose less to arbitrage
slides.text: LPs lose less to arbitrage. One-year lab backtest against a fixed-fee pool, on 1-minute ETH prices bridged to 12 s blocks. −27 % at the same average fee. −13 % at the same cost to traders. None of the storm’s 92 rolling 4-hour windows beats the replay (−18.6 %); median −2.1 %.
slides.notes:
Two honest comparisons from a one-year lab backtest on ETH. At the same average fee, clim's LPs lose 27 % less to arbitrage than a fixed-fee pool. At the same cost to traders, 13 % less. The 4 February replay you just saw is minus 18.6 %, and none of the 92 rolling 4-hour windows of that storm does better; the median window is minus 2.1 %. So the replay is a good day, not a typical one. In money terms: in the lab's main scenario, where an aggregator routes traders between the clim pool and a four times deeper 5 basis point pool, an ETH LP earns about 0.4 % of capital a year more than with a flat 5 basis point fee, about half of it in the five stormiest weeks: insurance, not a steady yield.

Sources (not read aloud): lab/out/backtest-summary.json and README Results: -26.9 % and -12.7 % (Oct 2025 to Oct 2026, 1-min data bridged to 12 s blocks); Feb storm -15.3 % and -2.9 %; 92 rolling 4 h windows from -18.4 % to +3.1 %, median -2.1 %, 66 of 92 beat the fixed pool; LP gain +0.39 %/yr in the main scenario (-0.10 % to +0.70 % across 5 scenarios), 53 % of it in the 5 stormiest weeks; lab/out/pstar_decision.json (aggregator scenario, 4x deeper static 5 bp pool).

slides.title: Not one more volatility fee
slides.text: Not one more volatility fee. This one predicts how often it gets arbitraged, and anyone can check. Share of blocks arbitraged, predicted and observed: Feb 2026 storm, 29.9 % and 27.9 %; Oct 2026 calm, 15.6 % and 17.1 %; one year (1-min data, bridged), 24.3 % and 23.6 %. Feb and Oct (1 s data): within 10 %, yet the gap is significant (p < 0.0005). Lab backtests.
slides.notes:
Fees that rise with volatility are not new: my design research counted at least fifteen, including LiquidMind, built on CRE at Chainlink's Convergence hackathon. What is new here is that the fee comes from a model that makes a prediction anyone can check: how often the pool gets arbitraged. In the February storm and the October calm, the observed share lands within 10 % of the prediction. The gap is still statistically significant, and I say so. And the model is right about how often, not how much: real losses run about 1.3 times its estimate.

Sources (not read aloud): spec section 11 (prior art: LiquidMind, Tempest, Bunni v2, Arrakis Pro, Alphix and Fables, Meteora DLMM, found in pre-hack and design research); lab/out/validation.json (p < 0.0005 with thresholds simulated from the model, because arbitrage comes in clusters); severity 1.29 to 1.33 in lab/out/summary.json.

slides.title: What is live on Sepolia
slides.text: Live on Sepolia since 6 October. {{LIVE_SEQ}} CRE reports on the live desk, about one every 30 s (RiskDesk seq, read {{LIVE_SEQ_READ}}). A real storm on 7 Oct, 02:11 UTC: σ at 242 %/yr, the fee at 26.5 bp. Built here: a CRE workflow, RiskDesk, ClimHook, bots, a lab, a dashboard. Try it: faucet, swap and liquidity at clim-zeta.vercel.app. CRE in simulation: one node, mock forwarder. DON deploy access was not granted in time.
slides.notes:
All of this runs on Ethereum's Sepolia testnet. Since 6 October at 16:26 UTC, my CRE loop has written about one report every 30 seconds to the live risk desk: {{LIVE_SEQ}} reports when I read it. In 36 hours I built the CRE workflow, the two contracts, the bots that trade on the clim pool and on a fixed-fee twin, the lab that chose the parameters, and the dashboard. And it has already met a real storm: on 7 October around 2 a.m. UTC, ETH moved fast, the desk's volatility climbed to 242 % a year, and the hook raised the fee on pool V to 26.5 basis points, then let it fall back to the floor within the hour. You can try it yourself: take test tokens from the faucet, swap, and add liquidity. The CRE workflow runs in the simulator, on one node; access to deploy it on a Chainlink network was requested but not granted during the hackathon.

Sources (not read aloud): the storm, from the live desk's RiskReported events: fee above the 5 bp floor from 01:58 to 02:51 UTC on 2026-10-07 (100 reports), σ peak 242 %/yr and fee 26.50 bp at 02:11 UTC; live RiskDesk 0xCDbfd6b9C0b97A8eE31706c6CDE5E54B4954334F (state().seq read {{LIVE_SEQ_READ}}); first report 2026-10-06 16:26 UTC; workflow in TypeScript compiled to WASM (cre/risk-desk), contracts in Solidity with Foundry tests (contracts/), bots in Bun and viem (bots/), Python lab (lab/), Next.js dashboard (app/); dashboard https://clim-zeta.vercel.app; verified on Sourcify ("match": same bytecode, metadata hash differs) for both desks, both hooks, tETH and tUSD.

slides.title: Rollout: one desk, many chains
slides.text: Fables on Robinhood Chain. One desk, many chains. 1: Shadow mode next to the Fables keeper, to tune the fee for fast blocks. 2: The Fables keeper reads the desk. 3: One report, on every chain CRE supports. Roadmap, our proposal to Fables: nothing runs on Robinhood Chain yet.
slides.notes:
A pool that is already live cannot gain a hook, but a DEX that already runs dynamic fees can use the desk without migrating. Fables does: its keeper, a bot that posts fee updates, raises the fee between a floor and a cap. Step one is shadow mode: clim publishes its fee next to the keeper's, and we tune it for Robinhood Chain's fast blocks, much shorter than Sepolia's 12 seconds. Step two, their keeper reads the desk and posts the fee, with no contract change on their side. Their keeper runs off-chain, so it can read a desk on any chain CRE writes to; today CRE lists Robinhood Chain only as a testnet. Step three, the same report goes to every chain CRE supports. This is my proposal to Fables, not an agreement: nothing runs on Robinhood Chain yet.

Sources (not read aloud): README Roadmap and Limits (fast chains: the formula sits at the floor until an effective block time is calibrated); spec section 5 (Fables: flat fee plus keeper pokeFee overrides, read from public on-chain data on 2026-09-30); CRE lists Robinhood Chain as a testnet only (docs, 2026-09-18); spec section 5.6 (a keeper is off-chain, so it can read a RiskDesk on any chain where CRE writes).

slides.title: Why it matters, and why Chainlink CRE
slides.text: Chainlink CRE, our only partner track, by choice. Insurance needs a weather station everyone trusts. At least three of four exchanges must agree. On a DON, once the owner renounces: no single key to steal. One number for many pools and chains. Today: CRE simulation on one node; our operator key submits the reports.
slides.notes:
Chainlink CRE is the only partner track I entered, on purpose: clim is a CRE workflow, not an integration bolted on, and without a fresh CRE report the hook falls back to its safe fee. Liquidity providers pay for every storm. A fee that follows the weather lets any pool, on any chain, charge for it. But insurance needs a weather station everyone trusts. The honest answer first: a volatility measured inside the pool would capture most of the gain in my backtests. Chainlink CRE is what makes the number trustworthy. Chainlink's own ETH volatility feeds use a 24-hour window with a one-hour heartbeat, so a one-hour storm barely moves them, and Data Streams are pulled by the user, so the swapper could pick which report to bring. CRE runs my own 15-minute estimate and pushes one report every 30 seconds. At least three of four exchanges must agree, so nobody can move the fee with fake trades on the pool. On a Chainlink network the nodes sign the report, and once I renounce ownership of the desk, there is no single key to steal. And one desk can serve many pools and chains. Today the workflow runs in simulation, and my operator key submits the reports.

Sources (not read aloud): README "Why Chainlink CRE" (in-pool volatility captures 54 % to 103 % of the gain, lab/out/summary.json); Chainlink's ETH realized-volatility Data Feeds have a 24 h shortest window and a 1 h heartbeat (docs/faq.md); Data Streams are pull-based, so the swapper picks the report (docs/faq.md, "Why Chainlink CRE, and not Data Feeds or Data Streams?").

slides.title: Appendix

slides.notes: The appendix holds the details behind the main slides: the fee rule, the live-pool question, safety, limits, the CRE evidence and the full demo video.

slides.title: Appendix: the fee rule
slides.text: The fee rule. fee = clamp(η · k · σ · √(Δt/2), floor, cap). σ: the desk’s 15-minute realized volatility. η: 1/P* − 0.824 = 2.51; P* = 30 % of blocks arbitraged above the floor. Δt: 12 s Sepolia blocks. k: model-risk multiplier from 1 to 2; k = 1 in this build. floor, cap: 5 bp (the pair’s usual tier), 150 bp. Milionis, Moallemi and Roughgarden (2023); Nezlobin and Tassy (2025).
slides.notes:
Sigma times the square root of half a block is the typical price move while an arbitrageur waits. Eta says how many of those moves the fee covers: with eta equal to one over P-star minus 0.824, a block gets arbitraged with probability P-star once the fee is above the floor. The lab chose P-star of 30 % against a competing 5 basis point pool before deployment, because the hook's parameters are immutable.

Sources (not read aloud): lab/scripts/decide_pstar.py and shared/params.json (etaE4 25093); on-chain integer arithmetic: fee_pips = clamp(ceil(sigmaE9 × etaE4 × sqrtHalfDtE6 × kE4 / 1e17), 500, 15000) in contracts/src/ClimFeeMath.sol; arXiv:2305.14604 and arXiv:2505.05113.

slides.title: Appendix: can a pool that is already live use clim?
slides.text: Can a pool that is already live use clim? Uniswap v3 pool: no, its fee is immutable. Uniswap v4 static-fee pool: no, create a new pool, LPs move. Dynamic-fee DEX, like Fables: yes, its keeper could read RiskDesk. clim’s own parameters: immutable, a new P* means a new hook. Details and sources: docs/faq.md in the repo.
slides.notes:
A Chainlink mentor asked this on day one. A Uniswap v4 pool's fee mode and hook are part of its identity, so a static-fee pool cannot become dynamic: you create a new pool and LPs move their liquidity. A pool created with a dynamic fee gets its fee from its own hook. A DEX whose keeper sets the fee, like Fables, could follow the desk with no contract change: its keeper would read it. A dynamic-fee pool's own hook can follow it only if the hook can read an outside source; otherwise it means a new hook and a new pool.

Sources (not read aloud): docs/faq.md ("Can a pool that is already live switch to clim?"), checked against v4-core and OpenZeppelin uniswap-hooks v1.2.1; spec section 5.6.

slides.title: Appendix: if the desk lies or goes quiet
slides.text: If the desk lies or goes quiet. Volatility jumps: capped per report, ×2 up, ×0.8 down. Silent for 180 s: blind, the fee is at least 30 bp. Exchanges disagree by more than 25 bp: degraded, the fee is at least 30 bp. A forged report: mined, ignored; today only our key can report. The owner: today also the only reporter, within the envelope; renounced after the switch to a DON. RiskDesk.sol and ClimHook.sol, with their Foundry tests.
slides.notes:
The desk rejects reports that come too fast, from the future or from fewer than three exchanges, and limits how far volatility can move between two reports. The hook charges at least a 30 basis point safe fee when the desk goes quiet for three minutes or when the exchanges disagree. A forged report I sent on Sepolia was mined and ignored by the desk. In simulation my operator key, which is also the owner, is the only accepted sender. So today my key does decide the volatility, within those limits: volatility can at most double or drop by a fifth per report, and the fee stays between 5 and 150 basis points. The owner role itself has no setter for the volatility or the fee. On a DON, the desk switches to the signed forwarder, simulation is disabled, and I renounce ownership.

Sources (not read aloud): contracts/src/RiskDesk.sol (20 s gap, 30 s future bound, quorum 3, x2 / x0.8 envelope, DEGRADED above 25 bp dispersion); contracts/src/ClimHook.sol (blind after 180 s, safe fee 3000 pips); forged report tx https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x34ee46a6947d2831fdb3e5a09f831008589efd9cf099f61dca86dc4cdadc53d9; on a DON: signed reports only, then disableSim() and renounce (README Roadmap).

slides.title: Appendix: limits
slides.text: Limits. Testnet only: CRE in simulation, our own bots make the market. The first move of a sudden jump is arbitraged at the old fee. LP gain against a 5 bp pool: −0.10 % to +0.70 % of capital a year. Arbitrage losses run 1.3 times the model’s estimate. In-pool volatility would capture most of the gain. Every 30 s on Ethereum mainnet: an estimated $60k to $110k a year in gas. Lab backtests on Binance ETHUSDT. Not audited. It is insurance, not a steady yield.
slides.notes:
These are the limits I would ask about as a judge. It is a testnet build: the workflow runs in simulation and my own bots make the market. The desk reports every 30 seconds, so the first move of a sudden jump is arbitraged at the old fee. The LP gain is real but modest. The model gets how often arbitrage happens right, but real losses run about 1.3 times its estimate. A volatility measured inside the pool would capture most of the gain, so CRE buys trust, not accuracy. And reporting every 30 seconds on Ethereum mainnet would cost a lot of gas, so production would publish on deviation or on a layer 2.

Sources (not read aloud): README Limits and Results; lab/out/summary.json (LP gain -0.10 % to +0.70 %, severity 1.29 to 1.33, in-pool share 54 % to 103 %); spec section 10 item 9 (design audit estimate); check: about 175k gas per report (median of the live Sepolia runs in bots/out/cre-runs.jsonl) times about 1.05 million reports a year is about 184 ETH a year per gwei, so $60k to $110k means about 0.12 to 0.22 gwei at $2,700 per ETH, before the production forwarder's signature checks.
